title: Jerome's Bible
hookLine: a grumpy genius in a Bethlehem cave translates the Bible into Latin
carry: ignorance of scripture is ignorance of christ

cards: Gourd, or ivy? A letter carries that question from North Africa to Bethlehem. Augustine is writing to Jerome.

A bishop in a town called Oea has had the book of Jonah read aloud in Jerome's new translation. At the moment God makes a plant grow up to shade the sulking prophet, the congregation hears a different plant.
They know it as a gourd. Jerome's version says ivy. There's an uproar in the church, Augustine says, and the bishop nearly loses his people over one word.

teach.b: Jerome was a scholar with a sharp pen and a short temper, and his letters show both. Tradition places him in Bethlehem, working near the cave where Christians remember Jesus being born.
Latin-speaking Christians already had Latin Bibles, translated from the Greek by different hands, and the copies didn't agree. Jerome set out to revise them, then did something bolder.
For the Old Testament, he went back past the Greek to the Hebrew. In his prefaces he calls it the Hebrew truth, and describes the hard labor of learning the language. That's how the gourd became ivy.
The Hebrew word for Jonah's plant is rare, and Jerome made a choice. When Augustine wrote, worried, Jerome wrote back, not gently, and defended it.

teach.h: GOURD OR IVY: A TRANSLATOR CHOOSES.
teach.b: The King James translators, also working from the Hebrew, went with gourd: "And the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head."
Readers still differ on what plant it was. Jerome's Latin went on being read and copied in the Western church long after him, and came to be called the Vulgate. And he gave a reason for the labor.

In his commentary on Isaiah he writes that not to know the scriptures is not to know Christ, echoing Jesus in John's Gospel: "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me."
A Bible in your own language comes through someone like Jerome, bent over a hard word, and getting letters about it.

how: Christians honor Jerome as a saint and a doctor of the church, and some remember him as a patron of translators; the Vulgate remains an official Latin text of the Catholic Church, while Christians today read the Bible in many modern translations.

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.

s: Jerome only polished the old Latin Bible
for the Old Testament he went back to the Hebrew, which he called the Hebrew truth.
one new word in Jonah caused an uproar in a church
Augustine wrote that a congregation in Oea was in uproar when the gourd became ivy.
everyone agrees exactly what Jonah's plant was
the Hebrew word is rare. Jerome chose ivy; the King James says gourd.

games.q: you're Jerome. a respected bishop writes that one word in your Jonah nearly cost a colleague his congregation. what do you do?
o: quietly change it back to gourd.
write back and defend your reading of the Hebrew.
give up translating: it's not worth the trouble.
games.why: Jerome wrote back and defended his choice, not gently, and kept working from the Hebrew.

practice: Think of someone who has carried words across for you: whoever put the Bible, or a book you love, into your language, a parent who interpreted at the doctor, a teacher or nurse who made a hard thing clear.
Picture them, and let a simple thanks rise. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, just hold the gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Vulgate. The Latin Bible tied to Jerome's work, made so people could hear scripture in the language of their own churches.
